> For the record: the Unabomber didn't advocate genocide or "murdering
> everyone", he just selected a few victims as "symbols". What he

No, I agree that he didn't advocate going out and killing everyone. He
did advocate "getting our attention" by murdering people. I have a
serious problem with the fact that he killed people for about 16 years
before he even came forward with his manuscript.  I also note that, of
the sixteen bombs, seven were not claimed as being by FC, and no hint
FC was made until the sixth bomb. The question of who are what FC was
didn't get resolved until 1995.  So, why did he not make his
ideological point, and make it clear that these were terrorist actions
with a purpose, from near the beginning?  Could it be that he merely
wanted to kill people, and only rationalized it years later?  I
consider that to be a serious possibility.

> advocates is getting rid of technology, although I'm not sure
> how. The 1971 essay merely advcates a halt to govt' funding for
> scientific research. Which might not be a

Well, I think he advocates a total "revolution" by society against
technology and against technological culture.  He advocates complete
physical destruction of anything related to high-technology.  He
argues that there are two forms of ideology, one for the "educated"
man and one for the "common" man:

  On the more sophisticated level the ideology should address itself
  to people who are intelligent, thoughtful and rational. The object
  should be to create a core of people who will be opposed to the
  industrial system on a rational, thought-out basis, with full
  appreciation of the problems and ambiguities involved, and of the
  price that has to be paid for getting rid of the system.[...]

  On a second level, the ideology should be propagated in a simplified
  form that will enable the unthinking majority to see the conflict of
  technology vs. nature in unambiguous terms.

This really conflicts with my personal beliefs and world viewpoint.  I
guess I would rank myself among the educated, since I am a liberal
arts student who has studied political science, philosophy, economics
literature, history, art, etc. But nothing I've seen has indicated to
me that the "common" man (these days, I guess that would be the people
not educated at the college level...) have less of a grasp on the
concepts or problems then I do.  Just because they don't spend their
time reading Marx (Karl or Leo "-), doesn't mean they can't see the
problems for themselves. Even if they don't, I'm not convinced that
any problems are so intricate that they can't be explained.

> Anyway, getting rid of technology would result in a lot of people
> dying because of humans' pathetic dependence on high-tech. But
> that's not quite the same as murdering everyone. A lot of people
> (such as Ted Kaczynski) would believe in learning to live simply and
> being less dependent on technology, because hell, we could have a
> crash any time and be forced to fend for ourselves.

Relevent quotes about this:

      So if the system breaks down it will do so either spontaneously,
      or through a process that is in part spontaneous but helped
      along by revolutionaries. If the breakdown is sudden, many
      people will die, since the world's population has become so
      overblown that it cannot even feed itself any longer without
      advanced technology. Even if the breakdown is gradual enough so
      that reduction of the population can occur more through lowering
      of the birth rate than through elevation of the death rate, the
      process of de-industrialization probably will be very chaotic
      and involve much suffering. It is naive to think it likely that
      technology can be phased out in a smoothly managed orderly way[...]

      In the second place, one has to balance the struggle and death
      against the loss of freedom and dignity. To many of us, freedom
      and dignity are more important than a long life or avoidance of
      physical pain. Besides, we all have to die some time, and it may
      be better to die fighting for survival, or for a cause, than to
      live a long but empty and purposeless life.

Gee, how cheerful and optimistic.  In another section he compares
technological man to an alcoholic on a keg of wine.  He argues that
the technological man simply doesn't have the will power to place
humanity and nature before gung-ho expansion of technology for profit.
I'm not at all convinced that he is right.  If you take this argument,
it essentially argues that there can somehow be a group of people who
"know" the dangers, and if only we follow them we will all be better
off.

Gee, I'm sure plenty of people from the Soviet Union and China could
tell us in detail what this can lead to.  Arguments like the
Unabomer's fail to understand a common problem with human beings: they
rarely realize how limited their understanding of the world is.  You
cannot possibly have a bunch of people who can effectively shape our
destinies and make everyone happy -- it simply doesn't work.  Along
similar lines, you can't have a "war council" which decides what "all
the right moves" will be in attacking technology, they are bound to
make a horrible mistake.  You take this, and add to it the fact that
they _expect_ problems and chaos, indeed that they view it as
necessary, and I believe you are bound to end up with a huge amount of
unnecessary suffering.

I also believe that any high-revolutionaries are bound to make a
power-play like what happened after the Russian Revolution, all for
the good of the people, of course.  Yeah, right.
